Here is the student checklist followed by the three rubrics. --- # Part 1: Student-Friendly Unit Checklist ## My Genetics Unit Tracker: From DNA to Traits **Name:** _______________________ **Period:** _____ *Use this page to track your learning over the next three weeks. Before each assessment, check off what you can do and note where you need extra practice!* ### Week 1: The Central Dogma (DNA $\rightarrow$ RNA $\rightarrow$ Protein) * [ ] **Base Pairing:** Given one strand of DNA, I can write the matching (complementary) DNA strand. * [ ] **Transcription:** I can turn a DNA sequence into a matching mRNA sequence. * [ ] **Translation:** I can use a codon chart to translate an mRNA sequence into a chain of amino acids. * [ ] **Structure & Function:** I can explain how the order of amino acids determines a protein’s 3D shape and job in the body. * [ ] **Modeling:** I can build or draw a model showing how DNA makes a protein, and I can point out one thing my model *doesn't* show well. ### Week 2: Inheritance, Pedigrees & Data * [ ] **Punnett Squares:** I can set up monohybrid (1-trait) and dihybrid (2-trait) crosses and calculate the chances (probabilities) of different offspring. * [ ] **Pedigree Detective:** Looking at a family tree (pedigree), I can figure out if a trait is dominant, recessive, or X-linked, and prove it using individuals from the chart. * [ ] **Genotype Guessing:** I can figure out the genotypes of specific people in a pedigree and explain why some might have an unknown second allele (like *A?*). * [ ] **Chi-Square ($\chi^2$) Math:** I can use class data to calculate expected vs. observed numbers, run a chi-square test, and explain if our results happened by random chance or if our hypothesis was wrong. ### Week 3: Mutations, Gene Expression & Ethics * [ ] **Spotting Mutations:** I can compare normal DNA to mutated DNA and identify if it’s a substitution, insertion, or deletion. * [ ] **Predicting Effects:** I can trace how a mutation changes the protein and explain why it might be harmful, helpful, or make no difference at all. * [ ] **Passing It On:** I can explain which mutations get passed down to offspring (gametes/sex cells) and which ones don’t (somatic/body cells). * [ ] **Gene Expression:** I can explain how the environment can turn genes "on" or "off" to change a trait without changing the actual DNA code. * [ ] **Bioethics & Policy:** I can explain the science behind a genetic technology (like CRISPR), look at it from at least two different people's perspectives, and use data to argue how it should be used. --- --- # Part 2: Single-Point Rubrics ## Assessment 1 Ask for help if you get stuck.* ### Week 1: DNA to Protein (Central Dogma) * [ ] 🔗 **Match DNA:** I can match DNA letters together (A with T, C with G). * [ ] 📝 **Make mRNA:** I can use a DNA strand to write the matching mRNA strand (A with U, C with G). * [ ] 🔍 **Read the Chart:** I can use a codon chart to find the right amino acids from mRNA. * [ ] 🧩 **Shape & Job:** I can explain how changing amino acids changes a protein’s shape and its job. * [ ] 🛠️ **Use a Model:** I can use a drawing or model to show how DNA makes a protein, and tell one thing my model is missing. ### Week 2: Family Traits & Math (Inheritance) * [ ] 🎲 **Punnett Squares:** I can fill in a Punnett square and find the chance (%) of a baby getting a trait. * [ ] 🌳 **Read a Family Tree:** I can look at a pedigree chart and tell if a trait is dominant, recessive, or X-linked. * [ ] 🕵️ **Find Letters (Genotypes):** I can write the gene letters (like *AA*, *Aa*, or *aa*) for people in a family tree. * [ ] 📊 **Check Data ($\chi^2$):** I can use the Chi-Square math steps to see if our class data matches what we predicted. ### Week 3: Mutations & Technology * [ ] ⚡ **Spot Changes:** I can look at DNA and tell if a letter was swapped, added, or deleted (mutation). * [ ] 🚦 **Good, Bad, or Neutral:** I can explain if a DNA mutation hurts, helps, or does nothing to the protein. * [ ] 👶 **Passed Down?:** I can tell which mutations can go to future babies (egg/sperm cells) and which cannot (body cells). * [ ] 🌡️ **Genes On/Off:** I can explain how things like environment or diet can turn genes "on" or "off." * [ ] ⚖️ **Right & Wrong (Ethics):** I can read about a gene tool (like CRISPR), share two sides of the story, and use facts to say how we should use it. --- --- # Part 2: Teacher Scoring Guides ## Teacher Guide 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model (20 Points) **Standards:** HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-2 | Criterion & Points | "Meets" Exemplar (Full Credit: 5 pts) | "Does Not Meet" Exemplar (Partial/Low: 1–3 pts) | Common Student Errors & Look-Fors | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **1. Model Accuracy**
*(6 pts)* | *Original:* TAC-CGA $\rightarrow$ AUG-GCU $\rightarrow$ Met-Ala.
*Mutated:* TAC-CCA $\rightarrow$ AUG-GGU $\rightarrow$ Met-Gly.
All base-pairing rules and codon translations are 100% accurate. | *Original:* TAC-CGA $\rightarrow$ ATG-GCT $\rightarrow$ Met-Ala.
(Uses T instead of U in mRNA, or translates directly from the DNA strand instead of mRNA). | • **Watch for:** Using 'T' in mRNA.
• **Watch for:** Translating the DNA triplets directly on the codon wheel instead of using the mRNA codons.
• **Watch for:** Re-starting translation instead of shifting frames on insertions/deletions. | | **2. Model Labels & Limitations**
*(4 pts)* | All molecules labeled. *Limitation:* "My paper model shows amino acids as flat circles, so it doesn't show how the protein actually folds into a 3D shape. I could use pipe cleaners to show folding." | Labels are missing or mixed up (labels mRNA as DNA). *Limitation:* "My model isn't very neat / I didn't color it." (Critiques artistic effort rather than scientific accuracy). | • Students often confuse artistic flaws with *scientific limitations*. Prompt them: "What happens in a real cell that isn't shown on your paper?" | | **3. Mutation CER**
*(6 pts)* | *Claim:* The deletion alters the phenotype.
*Evidence:* Deleting the 4th base shifts the reading frame, changing every amino acid after codon 1 and creating an early STOP.
*Reasoning:* A shortened chain cannot fold into the right 3D shape, so the enzyme cannot bind its target. | *Claim:* It changes the trait.
*Evidence:* The DNA changed from C to G.
*Reasoning:* Mutations are bad and break the protein so the person gets sick. (Skips the protein shape/function link). | • Students frequently jump straight from "DNA changed" to "Trait changed" without mentioning amino acids or protein shape.
• For silent mutations, make sure they state the amino acid *stayed the same*. | | **4. Heritability**
*(4 pts)* | "This mutation would only be passed to offspring if it happened in a gamete (sperm/egg cell). If it happened in a skin cell, only that person is affected." | "Yes, it will be passed down because it is in their DNA and babies get DNA from their parents." | • Students assume *all* DNA changes are heritable. Look for explicit distinction between somatic/body cells and gametes/sex cells. | --- ## Teacher Guide 2: Family Inheritance Investigation (20 Points) **Standards:** HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3 | Criterion & Points | "Meets" Exemplar (Full Credit) | "Does Not Meet" Exemplar (Partial/Low) | Common Student Errors & Look-Fors | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **1. Pedigree Pattern & Evidence**
*(5 pts)* | "This trait is autosomal recessive. Parents II-1 and II-2 do not have the trait, but their daughter (III-2) does. This proves the parents are carriers (*Aa*) hiding the recessive allele." | "It is recessive because not very many people in the chart have it, and it skips a generation." (No specific individuals cited; relies on "common vs. rare" myth). | • **Major misconception:** "Dominant = common, Recessive = rare."
• Require students to cite specific parent-offspring trios (e.g., unaffected parents having an affected child) as proof. | | **2. Genotypes & Probability**
*(5 pts)* | "II-1 is *Aa*, II-2 is *Aa*. Individual III-1 is *A?* (*AA* or *Aa*) because they are unaffected. If III-2 (*aa*) has a child with an *Aa* carrier, there is a 50% (2/4) chance the child has the trait." | Writes *AA* for all unaffected people without checking if they are carriers. Calculates probability by guessing rather than showing a Punnett square. | • Students forget that unaffected individuals in recessive pedigrees can be *AA* or *Aa* (Wait for *A?* notation).
• For X-linked traits, check that males only have one allele ($X^aY$, not $X^aX^a$). | | **3. Chi-Square ($\chi^2$) Analysis**
*(6 pts)* | Expected: 75 tall, 25 short. $\chi^2 = 1.33$. "Since 1.33 is less than the critical value of 3.84 (df=1), we fail to reject the null hypothesis. The difference between observed and expected is just random chance." | Uses observed numbers or percentages in the $(O-E)^2/E$ formula. "Our $\chi^2$ is 1.33, which proves our hypothesis is 100% true." | • **Math error:** Dividing by Observed ($O$) instead of Expected ($E$), or using percentages instead of raw counts.
• **Interpretation error:** Confusing whether $\chi^2 < \text{critical value}$ means the model fits or fails. | | **4. Family Letter**
*(4 pts)* | "Because you both carry a hidden copy of the gene, each baby you have has a 1-in-4 (25%) chance of having cystic fibrosis. This doesn't mean if you have 4 kids, 1 will definitely have it—each pregnancy is a fresh 25% roll of the dice." | "You are both heterozygotes so a monohybrid cross gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio. Your 4th kid will definitely get the disease." | • Watch for the "gambler's fallacy" (e.g., "You already had 1 affected child, so your next 3 will be fine").
• Check that tone is clear and avoids unexplained jargon. | --- ## Teacher Guide 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief (20 Points) **Standards:** ETS1.B, HS-LS3-2, SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information | Criterion & Points | "Meets" Exemplar (Full Credit) | "Does Not Meet" Exemplar (Partial/Low) | Common Student Errors & Look-Fors | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **1. Science & Unintended Risks**
*(5 pts)* | "CRISPR uses a guide RNA to find the mutated hemoglobin gene and Cas9 to cut the DNA. A major risk is an 'off-target edit,' where Cas9 cuts the wrong gene, potentially causing a new mutation that triggers cancer." | "CRISPR goes in and fixes bad DNA so you aren't sick anymore. A risk is that the surgery might hurt or cost too much." (No biological mechanism or genetic risk). | • Students often list *financial* or *social* problems as the biological unintended consequence. Make sure they connect the risk to **DNA/mutations/heritability** (e.g., off-target cuts, germline changes passed to future generations). | | **2. Policy Claim & Evidence**
*(6 pts)* | "The FDA should approve CRISPR for somatic cells in sickle cell patients, but ban embryo editing. In Source B, 29 of 30 sickle cell patients had zero pain crises after treatment, showing high efficacy, while Source C shows embryo edits have a 15% off-target rate." | "I think gene editing is good and should be legal because it helps sick people feel better, like the article said." (Vague claim, no specific data cited). | • Claims are often too broad ("CRISPR should be legal/illegal"). Push them to specify *conditions* (e.g., somatic vs. germline, fatal diseases vs. cosmetic traits).
• Check that at least one statistic/number from the packet is used. | | **3. Stakeholders & Trade-offs**
*(5 pts)* | "Patients want fast access to stop painful crises. However, bioethicists and insurers worry that at $2 million per treatment, only wealthy families will benefit, widening health inequality." | "Doctors want to use it to help people, and patients want to get cured." (Both stakeholders have the exact same viewpoint; no ethical tension or trade-off shown). | • Students tend to pick two stakeholders who agree with each other. Look for genuine *tension* between perspectives (e.g., innovation/cures vs. equity/safety/consent). | | **4. Counterargument & Rebuttal**
*(4 pts)* | "Critics argue we should ban all CRISPR therapy because of off-target mutation risks. While this is a valid safety concern, editing somatic bone marrow cells only affects one patient, not future generations, and for severe sickle cell patients, the proven relief outweighs the small risk." | "Some people say CRISPR is bad because it is 'playing God,' which is dumb because medicine always helps people." (Strawman counterargument; dismissive rebuttal without evidence). | • Students often write a weak counterargument just to knock it down easily, or they state a counterargument and forget to rebut it (accidentally contradicting their own essay). |
